task.goal: Help adult learners recognize misleading averages in a short public-health chart.
hard_constraints: One 50-minute class with 12 learners and printed charts; no internet or personal medical data.
Learners must compare mean and median without assuming prior statistics training.
Check transfer to a new chart and time spent, not just recall of definitions.
task.available_resources: Whiteboard and two anonymized example datasets.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Move one value: make the misleading average visible
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners physically rearrange printed value slips to see how one unusually large observation moves the mean while leaving the median relatively stable. This makes sensitivity to extreme values tangible before introducing terminology.

Prepare a short public-health chart and 12 value slips derived from the first anonymized dataset, preserving a relevant extreme value if one exists. Explain mean as an equal share of the total and median as the middle of an ordered line; demonstrate the even-number case. Learners work in four groups of three, ordering slips and calculating both summaries with guided arithmetic. They then replace the largest value with a clearly labeled hypothetical larger value and predict which summary changes. Groups annotate the chart with what its average reveals and conceals. Explicitly explain that neither summary is automatically misleading: the appropriate choice depends on the question, distribution, and labeling.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; common explanation, 8; assigned activity, 12; discussion, 8; individual transfer assessment, 10; feedback, 8. Keep the second dataset unseen until transfer. Its chart should use a different health measure and scale.

Needs: printed charts, slips, arithmetic scaffolds, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the datasets contain manageable numerical observations. If neither has useful asymmetry, use a labeled hypothetical modification for instruction, while acknowledging that transfer to strongly skewed data remains untested. This lesson addresses distributional distortion, not every possible chart problem.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign two groups to the manipulation activity and two to an equal-length worked example covering the same calculations. Before shared discussion, collect a brief independent explanation; treat the later transfer comparison cautiously because discussion may reduce differences. On the unseen chart, require each learner to calculate or locate mean and median, assess a headline, and explain which summary fits a stated question. Record completion time and unfinished responses at ten minutes. Score calculations and justified interpretation separately. The mechanism is weakened if manipulation produces no clearer explanation of extreme-value effects than the worked example, or only improves answers by requiring substantially more time. With 12 learners, results are descriptive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Audit the headline against the question
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach learners to evaluate an average as evidence for a specific public-health claim. The central action is checking whether a summary answers the question being asked, rather than spotting an unusual number alone.

Use the first dataset to prepare one short chart with its underlying values and two possible headlines: one about a typical observation and one about the total divided across observations. Both must be plausible enough to inspect, without implying either mean or median is always preferable. In four groups of three, learners complete an audit sheet: What is being claimed? What does each observation represent? What is the mean? What is the median? Which headline is supported, and what qualification is needed? Rotate reader, calculator, and challenger roles. Groups then rewrite one headline so its summary and scope are explicit.

Schedule: individual first impression, 5 minutes; plain-language instruction in mean and median, 8; assigned practice, 12; individual transfer, 10; comparison of reasoning, 10; corrective feedback, 5. Introduce the second dataset only during transfer, with a new chart, headline, units, and practical question. Ask learners to accept, qualify, or reject the claim and support their decision numerically.

Needs: printed charts, audit sheets, arithmetic guides, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the datasets have enough context to identify their observational units. Do not invent missing population or sampling information; mark those limits explicitly. This approach may improve claim evaluation while leaving independent calculation fragile, so both require assessment. Avoid teaching a shortcut that ‘typical’ always mandates the median.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign six learners to the audit sheet and six to a conventional calculate-and-define worksheet using the same first dataset and equal practice time. Give everyone identical instruction and the same individual transfer chart before discussion. Score correct mean and median separately from whether the learner connects the chosen summary to the claim and acknowledges a relevant limitation. Record each learner’s completion time, with a ten-minute cap and unfinished work retained. Include one transfer question for which the mean is useful, so blanket rejection of means fails. The audit mechanism is challenged if learners merely repeat cautionary language, cannot justify decisions using the new values, or perform no better than the comparator on claim evaluation. Offer the audit sheet to everyone afterward.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Predict, inspect, and revise a distribution
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: expose the information lost in a single average by asking learners to predict the underlying observations, then compare their predictions with the actual distribution. A mismatch creates a concrete reason to inspect both mean and median.

Start with a printed public-health chart showing only the mean from the first dataset. Ask learners to sketch where they expect individual observations to lie on a supplied number line; stress that several distributions could fit. Reveal the actual anonymized values on a second printed panel. Learners compare their sketches with the observations, order the values, and find the median. Introduce mean as equal sharing and median as the middle position, with a worked example and support for even-sized datasets. In pairs, learners explain what the original chart allowed them to infer and what it left uncertain. They revise its caption or add a small distribution display.

Schedule: prediction, 5 minutes; explanation, 8; assigned inspection activity, 12; individual transfer, 10; discussion and revision, 10; feedback, 5. Use the second dataset for an unseen chart with different units. Its assessment asks learners to distinguish conclusions supported by the mean alone from conclusions requiring the displayed observations, then compare mean and median once the observations are revealed.

Needs: paired printed chart panels, number-line sheets, whiteboard, arithmetic supports, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the source values are available and small enough to inspect on paper. Predictions are hypotheses, not errors to ridicule. The mechanism may be less striking when the first dataset is nearly symmetric; even then, multiple possible distributions remain a valid lesson.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign three pairs to predict before seeing the values and three pairs to inspect the same values immediately. Keep numerical instruction, materials, and total practice time equal. Assess transfer individually before group discussion. Score whether learners avoid unsupported claims about most observations, correctly compare mean and median, and use the revealed distribution to justify a conclusion. Record time separately for the mean-only judgment and the subsequent full-data judgment, within the ten-minute assessment window. The prediction step is not supported if it adds time without improving calibrated conclusions relative to immediate inspection, or if learners become indiscriminately distrustful even after adequate data are shown. Treat this small comparison as a classroom feasibility check, not a reliable effect estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repair a plausible mistake before it becomes a rule
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair incorrect worked solutions. Comparing a plausible error with a correct explanation could help them distinguish arithmetic mistakes from unsupported interpretations, and recognize those errors in a new chart. The active ingredient is explaining why a tempting solution fails.

Prepare a printed public-health chart and underlying observations from the first anonymized dataset. Add two clearly labeled fictional student solutions: one finds the median without ordering the values; another correctly calculates the mean but claims that most observations must equal or exceed it. Supply correct calculations separately for checking. Use actual dataset values; if the second claim happens to be true, explain that the mean alone still cannot establish it.

Use 5 minutes for an initial individual judgment, 8 for instruction, 12 for paired practice, 5 for individual explanation, 10 for unseen transfer, and 10 for discussion and feedback. Explain mean as total divided equally and median as the middle after ordering, including the two-middle-values case. During practice, six pairs identify the first unjustified step, repair it, and write a brief explanation that would help its fictional author. Emphasize that either summary can be useful, depending on the question.

Needs: printed charts, solution sheets, arithmetic guides, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Reserve the second dataset for transfer. Its chart must include sufficient observations to compare both summaries. Missing sampling context remains explicitly unknown. Incorrect examples require prompt correction; learners with fragile arithmetic may otherwise remember the error.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Assign three pairs to error repair and three to correct worked examples with equivalent explanation prompts and equal practice time. Before discussion, assess everyone individually on the second chart without fictional solutions: calculate mean and median, evaluate a claim about most observations, and explain an appropriate use of each summary. Record completion times and unfinished work at ten minutes. Score calculations and justified interpretations separately. The mechanism lacks support if repair learners repeat the planted errors, cannot transfer without error labels, or show no interpretation advantage over correct examples despite taking longer. Twelve learners provide a feasibility check, not a reliable effect estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Choose an average by seeing what a decision costs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners compare the consequences of using the mean or median as a planning number. Equal-sharing and typical-observation questions become concrete through two different measures of success: matching the observed total and minimizing total absolute distance from individual observations. This could replace the shortcut “one average is always better” with an understanding of why the question matters.

Use the first anonymized dataset and its public-health chart. Explain mean as total divided by count and median as the middle after ordering, including the even-count case. In four groups of three, learners calculate both using printed arithmetic guides. They then complete two paper challenges: multiply each proposed average by the observation count and compare with the actual total; calculate each observation’s distance from each proposed average and add those distances. Explain that distance means the positive gap, without introducing formal notation. The mean reproduces the total; the median minimizes total absolute distance, although ties are possible.

Groups annotate the chart with one question each summary helps answer and one conclusion the chart cannot establish. Clarify that minimizing numerical distance does not establish the best public-health policy, and a median need not be an observed value.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; instruction, 9; challenges, 14; individual unseen-chart assessment, 10; discussion and feedback, 13.

Needs: printed charts, calculation tables, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Reserve the second dataset for transfer. Assumes manageable numerical values with meaningful totals and differences; inspect this before teaching. Do not relabel observations or invent sampling context. If mean and median coincide, the exercise demonstrates agreement but provides weaker evidence about recognizing misleading averages.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give two groups the consequence challenges and two an equal-duration calculation worksheet with the same instruction. Before shared feedback, assess all 12 learners individually on the second chart: calculate mean and median, select a summary for each of two stated purposes, and judge a claim about typical observations using the displayed values. Record completion minutes and unfinished items at the ten-minute cap. Score arithmetic separately from justified interpretation. The mechanism is challenged if learners can complete the distance table but cannot select and justify summaries on transfer, or gain no interpretive advantage while taking longer. This small comparison assesses feasibility, not a dependable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Choose whether to judge or request more evidence
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach an evidence-sufficiency decision rule. Learners practice deciding when a chart supports a conclusion and when its missing information requires a specific request. This addresses a dependency of headline auditing: classroom charts may supply observations that real charts omit.

The instructor prepares printed versions of the first dataset’s public-health chart: one with underlying values and one without them. Introduce mean as the total shared equally and median as the middle after ordering, including the even-number case. Model calculating both with paper arithmetic.

Teach this action path: identify the conclusion; inspect the available information; calculate and compare both summaries when values are supplied; decide or qualify the conclusion; otherwise name the missing evidence and request it. A mean alone can support a statement about the reported mean, but cannot establish the median or how many observations exceed a threshold. Handoff means writing a request to the chart’s author, not contacting anyone. Recovery occurs when the instructor supplies the missing panel and learners revise their answer.

Use a close pair: the same claim about most observations, first with all values and then with only the mean. Include an unfamiliar case using the second dataset. Accept justified uncertainty about sampling or population scope even when calculations are possible.

Schedule: initial judgment 4 minutes; instruction 8; practice 12; individual transfer 12; recovery and feedback 14. Needs: printed panels, request slips, arithmetic guides, whiteboard and instructor timepiece. Assumes usable source values; missing contextual information stays explicitly unknown. The rule may encourage unnecessary deferral, so practice also includes a claim directly supported by the reported mean.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor owns one 12-person trial. After common instruction, randomly assign six learners to decision-rule practice and six to the prior headline-audit approach for equal time. Before discussion, everyone completes the same unseen assessment: a close pair on opposite sides of the information boundary and an unfamiliar chart from dataset two. Require calculation of mean and median where possible, a justified decision, and a precise request where necessary. Record completion time, unfinished work, unsupported conclusions and unnecessary deferrals. Provisionally retain the challenger only if it reduces unsupported conclusions without increasing unnecessary deferrals or median completion time; ties provide no evidence of improvement. Stop at 12 assessment minutes and retain partial responses. Give everyone corrective feedback. This small trial tests feasibility, not a reliable treatment effect.

EXPAND.title: Repair a plausible wrong solution
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair specific reasoning errors in completed examples. Seeing where a plausible method fails can help them distinguish a correct calculation from a defensible interpretation.

Before class, the instructor uses dataset one to prepare three short fictional solutions: one takes the middle entries before ordering; one calculates the mean incorrectly; one calculates both summaries correctly but claims that the mean proves most observations lie near it. Label these as practice solutions containing possible errors. Verify every intended correction beforehand. Provide the underlying values and a correct worked reference, revealed after learners attempt repairs.

Explain mean through equal sharing and median through ordered position, including even-sized lists. In four groups of three, learners inspect each solution, underline the first unsupported step, repair it and explain how that repair changes the chart’s message. Require them to accept correct steps, preventing a habit of rejecting everything. The instructor resolves disagreements on the whiteboard; learners then annotate the original public-health chart with a defensible statement.

Schedule: initial chart judgment 4 minutes; instruction 8; repair practice 13; individual transfer 12; correction and discussion 13. Transfer uses dataset two, different units and fresh wording. Learners calculate both summaries, evaluate one accurate explanation and one flawed explanation, and write their own conclusion.

Needs: printed charts, solution cards, blank calculation sheets, whiteboard and instructor timepiece. Assumes both datasets can support manageable paper calculations; long lists require preprinted ordered values or partial sums, with that support disclosed. If the summaries are similar, teach that agreement rather than manufacturing a distortion. The main limitation is possible dependence on recognizable errors, so the independent conclusion matters.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor runs one class trial, randomly assigning six learners to error repair and six to correct worked examples using the same dataset, numerical support and practice duration. Collect transfer individually before shared correction. Score mean and median calculations, acceptance of the accurate explanation, detection and repair of the flawed explanation, and the independently written chart interpretation. Record completion time and unanswered items at the 12-minute cap. Stop and reteach during practice if a group continues using an erroneous procedure after consulting the correct reference; record the intervention. Retain error repair provisionally only if independent interpretations improve without more calculation errors or longer median completion time. Otherwise prefer the simpler worked examples. With 12 learners, differences remain descriptive.

EXPAND.title: Make the explanation survive a listener’s questions
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: structured teach-back makes gaps in a learner’s explanation visible through another person’s attempt to use it. The listener must apply the explanation to actual observations, giving the speaker concrete feedback before independent transfer.

The instructor prepares the first public-health chart, its values, a calculation guide and listener cards. Teach mean as equal sharing and median as the middle of ordered values, including the even-number case. Learners calculate both individually, then check against a verified reference.

Form six pairs. In the first round, one learner explains what each summary says about the chart in everyday language. The listener points to values supporting the explanation and asks two fixed questions: ‘Does this tell us where the middle observation is?’ and ‘What can we actually conclude about most observations?’ The listener then writes a one-sentence interpretation based on what they heard. Speaker and listener compare that sentence with the data, identify any unsupported inference and repair the explanation. Switch roles using a second claim about the same dataset. The instructor handles unresolved numerical disagreements before transfer.

Schedule: opening judgment 4 minutes; instruction 8; calculation and verification 7; paired teach-back 12; individual transfer 12; feedback 7. Transfer uses the unseen second dataset: calculate mean and median, assess a new chart caption and write a short explanation for a reader without statistical training.

Needs: printed charts, value lists, listener prompts, calculation guides, whiteboard and instructor timepiece. No personal experiences or medical information are requested. Assumes learners can communicate in an accessible shared format; written exchanges can replace speaking. Pair agreement is not proof of correctness, so numerical references and individual transfer are essential. This route could improve explanation while slowing work or allowing a confident partner to dominate.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor owns a single-class comparison. Randomly assign three pairs to teach-back and three pairs to equal-time individual written explanation with the same numerical reference. All 12 take the identical individual transfer before discussion. Score calculations and evidence-based interpretation separately, including whether the explanation confuses mean with median or makes an unsupported claim about most observations. Record assessment completion time, unfinished responses and whether each teach-back participant completed both roles. Stop a paired round at its scheduled endpoint; instructor feedback repairs unresolved misconceptions afterward. Provisionally retain teach-back only if transfer interpretations improve without poorer calculations, longer median completion time or incomplete participation. If improvements appear only in rehearsed wording, prefer individual practice. The small, pair-assigned comparison cannot establish a dependable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Move one value: improved version of P0’s physical comparison mechanism
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: prior candidate 0, “Move one value.” This retains physical manipulation as its mechanism. The specific improvement is to separate sensitivity from misleading interpretation: after moving an extreme value, learners must explain whether the resulting average supports a particular chart caption. Movement alone does not establish that a chart misleads.

Preparation: the instructor verifies both datasets’ calculations and prints charts, value slips, arithmetic guides and answer sheets. Use manageable lists with their observational units stated. Explain mean as sharing the total equally and median as the middle after ordering, including averaging the two middle values. Twelve learners work in four groups of three.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; explanation, 8; slip activity, 12; interpretation discussion, 8; individual unseen-chart transfer, 12; feedback, 6. During the activity, groups calculate both summaries, predict the effect of changing the largest observation, then verify it. The altered value is explicitly hypothetical. They evaluate two captions: one describing the arithmetic mean and one claiming most observations are near it. Require support from the observations, rather than automatically rejecting the mean.

Transfer uses the untouched second dataset with a fresh public-health chart. Learners calculate mean and median, assess its caption and write a qualified replacement. The instructor records completion times. Feedback reveals the verified calculations and lets learners correct one unsupported inference.

Needs: printed materials, whiteboard and instructor timepiece; no internet or personal medical information. If the first dataset lacks useful asymmetry, use a clearly labeled hypothetical replacement during practice. If lists are too long, provide sums and ordered values while retaining comparison and interpretation. If the second dataset is nearly symmetric, assess recognition that the summaries agree; transfer to pronounced skew remains untested. Missing sampling context remains unknown.
EXPAND.experiment: Owner: instructor; first trial: this 50-minute class. Randomly give two groups P0’s original chart-annotation prompt and two the explicit caption-comparison prompt, with equal practice time. Score the same individual transfer for numerical accuracy and justified interpretation; record completion time and blanket rejection of means. Keep the improvement only provisionally if interpretation improves without slower completion or more blanket rejection. Stop and reteach if learners cannot distinguish the two summaries during practice. With only four groups, equal or worse results are sufficient to withhold a gain claim, not establish equivalence.

EXPAND.title: Design a selectively persuasive chart, then face its reader
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: constrained message production exposes why a numerically correct average can create a misleading impression. Learners experience choosing what to disclose and then observe what a reader infers. This differs from auditing a supplied headline: the learning event is the gap between the designer’s intended impression and the reader’s inference.

Preparation: the instructor verifies both datasets and prepares a chart template, value lists and two fictional communication briefs using dataset one: make its health measure appear relatively high or relatively low. Use this route only when mean and median differ enough to support those opposing impressions. All material is labeled classroom practice.

Schedule: initial interpretation, 4 minutes; plain-language mean and median instruction, 8; guided calculation, 7; designer–reader exchange, 12; debrief, 5; individual transfer, 10; correction, 4. Explain equal sharing, ordered middle and the even-number case without assuming statistics knowledge.

Form six pairs. Each learner designs a small chart using either the correctly labeled mean or median, with accurate units and a truthful caption. They may select information but cannot invent values or mislabel the statistic. Partners initially see only the chart and privately write what they infer about a typical observation. Reveal the full values and both summaries. Partners identify which inferences were supported, then jointly add the minimum disclosure needed to prevent the unsupported inference. The instructor resolves calculation disputes on the whiteboard.

Transfer uses dataset two, unseen until then: independently calculate both summaries, interpret a new chart and repair its caption if needed. Record elapsed time as well as answer quality. No personal health stories are requested.

Needs: printed charts, blank templates, arithmetic guides, whiteboard and instructor timepiece. If dataset one cannot support opposing impressions, use a supplied, explicitly hypothetical modification for design practice, preserving dataset two for transfer. Numerical separation alone does not prove misleadingness; the reader’s inference and the question determine that. This route may reward persuasive shortcuts unless the disclosure repair and debrief are completed.
EXPAND.experiment: Owner: instructor; bounded trial: one class. Randomly assign three pairs to designer–reader practice and three to ordinary calculation-and-caption evaluation using the same data and 12-minute allowance. Give everyone identical individual transfer. Compare justified interpretations, completion time and unsupported claims that one statistic is always preferable. Stop the design exercise at 12 minutes and supply a verified disclosure example if repairs remain unfinished. Retain the route only provisionally if transfer improves without more blanket rules or unfinished responses; no improvement or greater confusion would argue against its added complexity. The small trial cannot establish superiority.
